The treble roll-off is really lovely: nothing pierces or sticks out pointy at any particular frequency. The mid-bass isn't as high as the Ling Long, nor the sub-bass, so it's less bassy than the Ling Long. If you like balanced, cleaner-sounding, not muffled/bassy, take this, and get the DSP version with the USB-C plug.

Widest stereo imaging, most comfortable ANC, king of bean-shaped TWS "Oh, the timbre in the mids. Crank it up and it's insanely natural: dynamic-driver timbre that's very studio-monitor-like. Front-to-back depth and top-to-bottom dimension feel even bigger. Not as bright as the Buds 3 Pro and MTW4, though. The ANC blocks people talking even better, yet it's still comfortable; 8 ANC mics in a TWS is crazy. The mic improved too. Only the price is heavy. The bean-shaped TWS to beat, hands down. (Full review on his YouTube.)"

King of soundstage, amazing vocal timbre, superb mic "The vocal timbre is great. Very clean, wide and clear. Front-to-back depth and top-to-bottom staging are much better than the Buds 3 Pro. The planar timbre is much better than the 3's. Still the king of transparency mode. ANC is better than the 3's. Downside: replacement eartips are still hard to find."

Superb mic; iOS/Android/Windows ready, no ecosystem lock-in "Samsung won't open multipoint to iOS or non-Samsung Android; here nothing is locked. The app is on iOS, Android and even macOS. Sound is broadly like the Buds4 Pro but with more around 500 Hz; very mid-forward overall (watch his YouTube review). EQs fine. Technicalities are great too, but for natural timbre Samsung and Sony are still the champions in my view. The planar timbre here is still a little less natural, but far better than the metallic, pointy FreeBuds Pro 4."

King of soundstage, king of transparency, superb mic "Best price for every feature you need! Open-sounding soundstage that's outside your head, amazing, open-back style. 1 DD + 1 planar. U-shaped, a bit bright. King of transparency: super clear, like you're not wearing TWS at all. ANC comfort isn't Sony level yet but it's fine. The mic is ridiculously clear. Downsides: the slide volume control is a bit fiddly, and the codec is nerfed (supposedly only good with Samsung's SSC), but honestly AAC on my phone was fine too. The drivers are just nice. Ultra-HQ codecs aren't that important if the driver is good. Other downside: the eartips are squarish and hard to find. (Full review on his YouTube.)"

Killer of all flagships "Fantastic quality for the price. Good timbre. Soundstage and imaging are spacious. The September 2026 firmware adds PARAMETRIC EQ. Sub-bass slam rumbles deeper than the regular 4 and can rival the H3. Wide separation. ANC is quiet and its noise response keeps getting better. Battery lasts forever. (Full review and comparison on his YouTube.)"

Hard to beat. aptX Lossless, 52-hour battery, good mic, OK ANC, Auracast, under a million rupiah. On features alone it's hard to beat. Sound is fine too: the treble is safer than the Air 2 and Air 3, which have a bit too much and are a little spicy. The Free Pro 3 is slightly warmer with nice timbre and a touch wider imaging, but overall I prefer this tuning; its mids are better. The FP3 loses on ANC, mic, battery, codec and features. If you want it all, nothing under a million beats this. Round eartips, not square or keyed like Huawei's and the L4NC's. (Full review on his YouTube.)

World-class ANC "I underestimated it at first because the QC Ultra was too V-shaped, even with EQ. This one's default tuning has good timbre and feels grand. The bass is deep, and surprisingly there's a nice vocal emphasis too. Not as bright as the Accentum either. Out of the box, no EQ, it sounds super good and will satisfy non-hobbyists and hobbyists alike. Downside: no aptX, so very sensitive listeners may want a bit more treble clarity. The ANC has NO RIVAL, sorry: at 2 million rupiah its ANC can beat even the XM5. The mic is a bit weak in crowded places. (Full review on his YouTube.)"

No compromise, price dropped "One of the most advanced ANCs: naturally quiet, with lots of customisation. Two chips and three feedback mics with a great wind cover that pick out and suppress sound very well. Sounds better than the XM4 with the new Driver X: more clarity, cleaner vocals, a wider soundstage and vibrating bass rumble. Better mic than the XM4 as well. (TWS battle review on his YouTube.)"

Sound quality is more or less the same as the 3. The timbre is better: the mids aren't buried as much. But the treble is still a bit bright; you can still hear ringing and sizzle. It's OK. EQ still doesn't work unless Android's Absolute Volume is turned on. I'm sure the mic is fine judging from YouTubers' reviews; I couldn't test it, I only tried it at a mall. ANC isn't much different: highs still get through, not Sony or Bose level. But the 3 will surely be discontinued, so like it or not, this is where you go.

Great value, great mic "U-shaped. VERY GOOD IMAGING: height, depth, width. Airy and very open sounding. ANC is very decent and quiet, though I think the LinkBuds and Bose QCE are still better. Immersive, with a wide-open soundstage and imaging; clean, a bit bright. Less punchy than Sennheiser, but the imaging and soundstage are spacious if you like a slightly U-shaped tuning. Well priced too. The timbre is a bit unnatural."

It destroys the value of overpriced TWS like Jabra, JBL and Marshall. A Knowles balanced armature + single DD with an active crossover. Crunchy, aggressive mids. A really good microphone. The most advanced parametric EQ. Deep ANC. 4 mics on each bud for calls. Downsides: a bit sharp at the top of the treble, 10 kHz and up; the mids are a bit recessed. Edifier needs to make its custom EQ even better.

Budget technicalities "Wow, this is the bean-shaped version of the EarFun Air Pro 4. Wide, good separation, good imaging, and best of all the sub-bass extension is deep and really fun, but not basshead either. Loses on battery, and the timbre is plasticky compared to the Air Pro 4. He covers everything in his video."

Just so-so. V-shaped and a bit bright, still like the NeoBuds Pro 2. Better with EQ: the Classic/Classical preset (I forget which) is already an improvement. Codec is still only LDAC, no aptX Lossless in 2024. Mic is OK. But there's no multipoint like the NeoBuds Pro 2. Battery is very strong, but the official site doesn't say how long it lasts with ANC on.

Best-sounding bean shape "It wins if you like the bean shape. I think the Space Travel 2 is right on value and price, but its case doesn't close; this one's does. Boomy in the sub-bass, bright around 8–11 kHz, but it has an 8-band parametric EQ. Mic is not bad, better than the 4i. Separation and soundstage are better than the 4i / 4 Pro / Aerosound 6. ANC is better than the 4i, 4 Pro and Aerosound 6."

Jack of all trades "LDAC, multipoint, 50-hour battery, 3 AI mics, custom EQ. The sound isn't sharp and piercing any more like the regular Liberty 4. Adaptive ANC, super deep and silent, and adjustable. Superb transparency with dual vocal/ambient modes. The sound still leans bassy, but the treble doesn't pierce any more. (Full review on his YouTube: TWS from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)"

Classic Sony: the bass, the space. The texture, depth and width are a bit different from Sennheiser, and so is the resolution. I prefer the CX Plus. Both are warm, but this one's technicalities are drier: you still don't quite get the reverb tails and midrange detail. The WF-C500 sounds on par with this, or even better. (TWS battle review on his YouTube.)

It has LDAC and the best ANC technology, with auto ANC and a custom EQ. Basically great: as a Sony fanboy this is a must-have. Its LDAC is the most stable, not buggy, and not as battery-hungry as the NeoBuds and Liberty 3 Pro.
Bright, too bright: I can't cut the air treble. The Aerosound 6 Pro's treble is much safer. Skip it; same price anyway.

Poor man's AirPods "Right for a consumer with a budget who doesn't want a lot of fuss: wants the AirPods stem look but cheap, no logo on the body, and good. Good mic, proper ANC. The sound is just balanced and safe. Mic is better than the Free Pro 3, fit is fine. Tuning and technicalities: the Free Pro 3 is nicer once EQ'd. Not basshead like the P40i or Liberty 4 NC either. ANC is quieter than the L4NC."

Sounds good, and EQs really well. Timbre and stage are good compared with the SoundPeats Mini or even the Capsule 3 Pro. Its weakness is no ANC, that's all; if something's lacking, just boost it. The mids are clean and pretty. Its strength is the sound. Already beaten by the EarFun 4i. (Full review on his YouTube: TWS from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)
Sounds good, very bassy though. Wide soundstage. But the fit is too big. My advice now: get the EarFun Free Pro 3 instead. This one's discontinued.

More or less the same as the Ear 2. The tuning is ordinary, but people love it for its indie transparent look and want affirmation of the sound. Nothing's driver isn't bad (DMS says the same), but as a gadget its options are very lacking in my personal opinion. The EQ is a mess: switch EQ on, still flat, and suddenly the sound changes, gets patchy and weird, and the volume drops. If you like the default tuning, go for it. Mic is not bad. There, you've got your affirmation.

The ANC is interesting: Strong, Mild and pass-through, so you can hear your surroundings while listening. The Strong ANC is nice too. You can assign gestures freely: what tap-and-hold, double tap and triple tap do.

KING OF MIC at 200k. A clear driver, brighter than the Clear; the Clear's highs are smoother, warm, smooth and lush, while this one's more aggressive. The bass rumble is also wider and punchier, but not as murky and boomy as the R50i NC. Has ANC, light, about R50i NC class. EQ presets can be shared between users; I'll make one. Sound is in the same class as the Clear; it comes down to preference. I'm sure many budget buyers will prefer this, because the Clear feels more neutral and smooth while this is brighter and hits more fun. (Full review on his YouTube.)

40-hour battery with a serious custom EQ: you can cut bass from 125 Hz down to 30 Hz and below, so it won't be as BOOMY as the Eggel or the Soundcore R50i and A20i. You can raise the volume further on the TWS even when the phone is at max. Gaming mode, app support. (Video review on his YouTube.)

King of battery, without sacrificing the sound: really good. Shame about the price; at around 2.2 million it might be more popular. A less-known name, but it sounds good. Sadly no ANC for those who need it, but it has transparency.

More complete features than the regular R50i. The noise cancelling is real, not a gimmick, but still very light; I'd strongly recommend the Dot 3i. The sound is an improvement over the Dot 3i, but for technicalities and tuning I prefer the SoundPeats Clear. Mic is OK (4 AI mics), the battery is upgraded and the case doubles as a phone stand, which is unique. Get this if you don't need great sound, love lots of bass, and want to try ANC. (Full review on his YouTube: TWS from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

A sound upgrade over the Z3: the low-mids and bass are more correct, not too boomy. Has ANC, and it's not bad. Sound is OK and it gets really loud. The battery isn't as big as the Z3's any more, though, since it now has ANC.

Shouty and sharp. It can be EQ'd (see his EQ table) to be better. The treble is a bit grainy and rough; it's a SoundPeats driver after all. But you can reduce the bass so it isn't too boomy or muddy. Battery lasts forever. LDAC. Mic is decent. 80 ms latency, better than the Air Pro 3. If you don't care too much about sound it's actually not bad at all, and fairly affordable.
Hard to place against other consumer TWS, and the price doesn't help. (Full review on his YouTube.)

Main weakness: battery. The tuning is lovely. Technicalities are a little lacking in detail and soundstage, and treble extension is a bit short. The rest is fine. 55 ms game mode at a very low price. Sounds nice without custom EQ. Mic is ordinary. Also, the case has no lid. (Full review on his YouTube: TWS from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)
Skip to the Engine 4, Dot 3i or Air 2.
Sounds good. Has a custom EQ. Fairly bassy. Fit is a bit trickier than the Dot 3i. The mic is truly unusable, really bad compared with the Dot 3i.

This is good, and the EQ is good: sensitive, even 1 dB is clearly audible. A properly great EQ. ANC is not Sony level. The sound has a lot of lower mids, bunched up; that's why I EQ it down so the vocal midrange is clearer and not muddy. And the EQ really works. The bass timbre is very OK too.

7 + 70 hours of battery, absolutely insane. The sound is also very OK, very good value and powerful. Good tuning, not shouty; people will surely love the bass, though the soundstage isn't very grand. The WATERPROOFING is crazy: you can drop it in a glass of water and it's fine. (He suggests trying a demo at CSI Zone, Pamulang.)

Tuning OK, driver OK. Sadly the Bluetooth codec is still AAC/SBC; with aptX on the same driver the vocal and cymbal detail would be even better. Has ANC. The voice prompts when you switch ANC modes, connect etc. sound like an anime girl character. The driver and tuning sound so good, and punchy. Low volume. The app isn't great.

Neckband with custom EQ "A good neckband. Good mic. Balanced sound, better than Sony's wired in-ears under 300k rupiah; this is the better buy. Has custom EQ, play/pause/next/previous and volume controls, and Sony-style DSEE upscaling. Trust me, this is nicer than the XB400, which can't even be EQ'd in Sony's app."

Lots of people ask. A bit muddy, bassy, no custom EQ, a very ordinary mic. Its strengths: the Samsung name, plus OK ANC and fit. Why is the ANC OK? Because the fit is: it seals the ear really well and has an extra rubber fin to close the seal. Good passive isolation, good ANC. The rest, not really. Only for people who need ANC and don't care about EQ; you don't need me to convince you. If you like it, just buy it. Totally fine. Done.

Sound is decent and EQable, but the EQ isn't practical: you have to save before you hear the effect. Limited controls: changing volume means no play/pause, only double and triple tap. ANC is there, that's about it. Not recommended. At this budget, skip ANC; better a big battery like the SoundPeats Clear.

Warm, wide in the bass and low-mids. A murky driver, though not as murky as the T3. Not stunning. Wide in the bass. Of the 22 EQ presets, only Piano, Bass Reducer and Treble Booster are usable. Good mic, but the Nakamichi TW018S's mic is better. (Full review on his YouTube: TWS from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)
Skip to the R50i NC.
Not worth reviewing. Bad. Incoherent. The highs are too tizzy. At 1.9 million rupiah you'd be buying something far too overpriced. Maybe only for weeb collectors, or as a fashion accessory.

Good imaging, clear separation, like there's wide space to the left and right. The tonality is very neutral. The bass is present, but the fit doesn't grip much. Flathead style; maybe long-time earbud fans who want a TWS will accept this. Quite neutral, with a lot of lower mids in my view. If you just want a cheap TWS with lots of features and a good mic, the K20i is more than enough.

Tonally OK, actually; the bass preset is fine too. But the volume is low, not as loud as EarFun; especially outdoors with traffic noise it's surely not great. Good timbre, good driver, mic not bad. AAC codec.

Highly coherent + superb natural timbre and stereo imaging width "CAN'T GO WRONG WITH Xenns: the best DD and BA implementation, pushed to the max. The timbre is definitely more natural, far less plasticky than the regular Tea Pro. The mid-bass is cleaned up: lowered, but you still feel it. The 2 DDs now rumble just right, not as bassy and slightly muddy as the Tea Pro. Annoyingly, the treble rises again from 6 kHz up, so it's best at medium-to-low volume. The 2 Knowles BAs are upgraded in the highs, but I think the boost should have stayed at the Tea Pro's amount."

You can't go wrong with this set. A bit more sub-bass than the Tea Pro. The treble goes in a similar direction to the Tea Pro SE, but the highs have an appealing smoothness and sharpness. The soundstage up top is indeed wide, but the Tea Pro SE's stereo separation and imaging are wider. The sense of room can compete, but for stereo imaging width the Tea Pro SE is still the champion. Vocals are more forward and cleaner on the Tea Pro SE. This one is good in the highs, but the imaging is still a little centred for the budget.

Holographic imaging and stage (Iga Massardi, Gerald / Barasuara) "ENDGAME UNDER 10 million rupiah for me, subjectively. Coherency better than the Hype 4, Davinci, Oracle 3 and EJ07M. Proper bass, not overdone but still fun compared with the Pilgrim Silver. The vocals stay separate from the bass even though the bass spreads wide, deep and punchy; it doesn't bleed into the vocals. Like a stage PA: bass sent via aux to the sub, vocals stay in the mains. Separation and soundstage better than the Tea 2, with more clarity too. Volume linearity is solid even loud, typical Mangird. Spacious and pleasant. No need to swap the cable (it's detachable). Definitely worth more than its price. (Review on his YouTube.)"

Clean tactile bass! "A very unique configuration. The good bone-conduction driver I found really impressive is in the Canpur CP622B, but I don't put those in the book because they're too expensive for my audience; let's keep it below 10 million. But this is good, tidy. The bass is tight, cushioned, cleaner than the Tea Pro, bouncy but clean, less boomy/bloated, faster than the Tea Pro. The treble is dangerous from 6–8 kHz to 14 kHz, making the treble and air bright. Very good separation; it competes strongly with the Tea Pro. I think the soundstage is slightly better than the Tea Pro. The fit is bigger and fuller in the ear than the Tea Pro."

Asteriska & TJ (Barasuara) "Good timbre, good coherency. The only problem for me is the treble: the top end is a bit pointy. If you listen loud and are sensitive above 10 kHz it may be too airy, though some people like this; I don't much. I want the upper mids to treble like JM-1 or a Meta tuning, falling gradually rather than climbing again (see the JM-1 curve on squig.link/lab/fernandagunsan). Overall the timbre is more correct and less plasticky than the Tea Pro, but I don't hear an improvement in imaging or soundstage; the bass and mid-bass are cleaner. If you want something that feels clean and less bassy than the Tea Pro, this could be it. But remember the treble rises at the very top: not in the shouty/sibilant 4–8 kHz area, but 10 kHz and above."

King of separation at 2 million rupiah "Instrument separation, and the left-right spread, reach a bit further than the Daybreak and T6; both can still match its soundstage space. The main weakness is the timbre of the highs: still a bit metallic and crispy (even after EQ), so hi-hats and cymbals sound less natural. The kick has depth; the bass goes fairly deep too, wide and solid. Coherency is far above the Defiant: very unified."

Very balanced. Not as blunt as the Tea 2. The bass punch is right in quantity and quality: not a lot, but just right, with more rumble than the 41T or Tea 2, though not as much as the Tea Pro. Good imaging; the soundstage is right there with the Tea 2 and cheaper. Cleaner mids. Very natural sound. The timbre is OK, not as plasticky and blunt as the Tea 2. More fun and less neutral than the Tea 2 or 41T, but not basshead either; just right. Weaknesses: the fit is actually fine, it just needs the right eartips; and I wish the separation had more contrast. But at this budget it's crazy good. (Review on his YouTube.)
New, recommended "Good. JM-1 target. Better timbre and fit than the Daybreak. Technicalities slightly better than the Daybreak, but the price is waaay higher, bruv. (Full review on his YouTube.)"

SUPERB IEM FIT, and versatile with its cable: swappable 3.5 / 2.5 / 4.4 mm plugs, very practical. Smooth sound in the upper mids; the treble is sparkly but smooth, not aggressive, not piercing. Good timbre too for an all-5-BA set. Good punch, fast sub-bass, though a shame it doesn't go quite deep enough without a DD. But the fit is too good to skip, and the sound is very friendly for monitoring!

FINALLY, A MINI TEA 2! Warm-balanced, tuned very much like the Tea 2. Where the SR5 has some sharpness at 8 kHz and lacks lower mids, this has none of that. The 4BA + 1DD tuning that suits me best, and very nice for monitoring too: accurate, good imaging and soundstage, though not as aggressive, crunchy, wide and spacious as the Tea 2. Is it better than the SR5? For me, yes. Some might miss the 8 kHz treble brightness. The fit is AMAZING for monitoring; no need to swap cables or tips. (Review on his YouTube.)

Good. Neutral, natural midrange, with more vocal emphasis and a fairly boosted treble sizzle, though not as boosted as the Supermix 4. The transition from upper mids/treble down to the lows is lacking a little: not quite full-sounding. Coherency is actually OK but could be better; people who can't hear coherency much may not notice. It's good: natural, a lovely faceplate, and the fit works well on stage.

A 4-way crossover, HIGHLY COHERENT: not messy, no patchiness or missing frequencies. For 2 million rupiah, 5 drivers this coherent. Bright at 8 kHz: a tad of boost there, not piercing but dominant. Smooth top-end treble on cymbals, clear, not aggressive. Good midrange; guitars sound aggressive. KNOWLES BA, BABY! The sub-bass boost isn't big but the DD quality is superb: deep and thick. Sub-bass-centric (under 80 Hz), not much mid-bass around 100–150 Hz. Lovely vocals, and the bass comes through. (Review on his YouTube.)

Lovers of very forward vocals plus lots of sub-bass, while still balanced and not basshead, can take this. Very Gizaudio tuning: deep, plentiful sub-bass, but it can't be called basshead yet. The nicest thing is the fit: its shape hangs in the ear rather than hugging it like the SR5.

Now this is the best planar I've tried so far. No need for the Timeless any more, or the Raptgo, TRN Kirin or Tin P1. Just this. Pleasant, bright and clear, lovely, and the soundstage technicalities are extraordinarily good: holographic, fast, crunchy. Great for vocals, all genres, fast bass. For rock with distortion, fuzz and overdrive it's insanely good. The space: the reverb and soundstage are really grand. With AET08 tips the treble comes down to just right: not painful, but not lacking either.

Good stage, good timbre "Basically the same as the Tin T6 with the pink nozzle; the tuning isn't far off. The T6's soundstage is a tiiiny bit better, with more dimension forward and upward. This one's fit is better: full resin, no metal like the T6. You can't swap nozzle filters, and the cable is 2-pin, not QDC. The timbre is more natural and smooth, less metallic in the highs, even when both are EQ'd to the same target. Your choice; both are good."

NATURAL TIMBRE DYNAMICS! Clear separation, natural timbre, grand and luxurious. A bit hard to drive. Better than the DZ4 and C3, and I find its natural treble timbre nicer than the Sonus. The Sonus is in the same class, but I prefer this one's imaging. BA treble vs DD treble is personal taste, but the Sonus has a bit less mid-bass. This is thicker but not muddy, and safer from shoutiness than the Sonus (and even then you have to push the Sonus very loud before it's shouty). Its weakness: a bit hard to drive. (Review on his YouTube.)

This, the EW300 and the Xuan NV are the same class. The best bass if you want fun: rumble, bass timbre, good bass technicalities, plus really lovely treble breadth and openness. Volume linearity: it doesn't need to be as loud as the Xuan NV. If you like it loud, the Xuan's treble is safer. The fit is far better than the Xuan and EW300. Two followers DM'd me saying it easily develops channel imbalance (you've been warned); I've only tried it in a shop. Fun and technically very good. The DD timbre is slightly less flat than the Xuan: more sparkle and more bottom end than the Xuan, but the treble sizzle isn't as metallic as the EW300. Skip the BL02: too V-shaped with metallic timbre.

Still very Moondrop: the upper mids rise early from 1 kHz. The VDSF target, with nasal mids and very high vocals in the midrange. Moondrop drivers are never bad; the tuning is just the same as usual. Not bad, there's a market for it. The Ref version is more neutral; the Pop version has more mid-bass to sub-bass.

The tonality is very close to the Kinera Wyvern Black/White, with a small low-mid bump due to the bone conduction inside the shell (it's a low-frequency driver; it doesn't vibrate like Shokz, it just adds sub-bass extension), but the bass quantity doesn't grow much. It won't be like the bone conduction in the 50-million Canpur. The mic is better: louder, 4 mic gain levels, and mic noise reduction too, though I think the Rays does it better. For the price it's OK for gamers and casual South-Jakarta-office-worker meetings. The colour isn't gamer-y either: black.

Includes a DSP EQ dongle DAC "This is actually OK. The tuning is similar to the EW300, with a lot of top-end treble that can be dangerous. But it comes with a dongle DAC with an 8-band parametric EQ, and a mic whose gain you can set in the app. Cool, Simgot: I thought the app couldn't rival FiiO/Moondrop, but it's really good. Shame the DAC's amp is small, like the Moondrop Echo; something like the Akliam PD6 might be wider, but then the price might not work. Mid-bass to sub-bass is also similar to the EW300 or LM500: the mids dip around 800 Hz and rise gradually from the low-mids to the sub."

New "A very upper-mid-to-lower-treble-centric type, so it's clear and forward in the vocals. If you're after very natural timbre, I think there's still a hint of metallic shrillness around 4–6 kHz. It's sort of the counter to the EW300, which has lots of sub and top treble but mids/upper mids that don't fill in much; the Sublimation instead bites with really bold upper mids to lower treble."

ER4XR "THE ONLY REAL NEUTRAL IEM. Only this one. Not the Dunu Titan S, not the HZSound Mirror. No. Only this. Its only weakness is the deep insertion; if you're not used to it, it's uncomfortable. But that's the technology that makes the treble roll-off right and neutral."

No problem with the tuning: a little in the direction of the 61T. But coherency is lacking: the low-mids go missing, with a lot of vocal emphasis. And the timbre is pretty bad, very plasticky, losing the definition you usually get from multi-BA IEMs at 3 million rupiah and up. The mids aren't tight, not well defined, not unified. The tuning's OK. If you only need the looks and the tuning, go ahead. My choice is still the trio: Xuan, EW300, Soratune.
Same as the Inawaken Dawn MS; just a different faceplate, as far as I can tell. Feel free to take this or not, or step down to the Dawn MS. Very similar.

Good driver. Tuned like the Inawaken Dawn MS, the type where the mid-bass rises early, but the bass recovers from its impact a bit slowly, so it seems to have a lot of mid-bass to sub. If you want clean mid-bass, this isn't a good fit; go to the Xuan NV or Soratune. Not as airy as the EW300 either. Average soundstage and imaging, but decent for the price.

The first single planar I could enjoy on first listen without a lot of excuses about flaws. The sub-bass is OK, a bit much, but fast because it's planar. Very enjoyable. Crunchy electric guitars, a wide, open stage. I think it needs a bit more power to sound its best. SUPERB CLARITY: very clear even on murky/warm recordings. More sub-bass than the Heyday version.

Very transparent mids; a lovely, clean midrange, properly neutral with a sub-bass boost. The mid-bass is limp, not punchy, lacking weight. A spacious, open soundstage compared with the stock Dawn MS and C3. The weakness: not enough mid-bass for mid-bass lovers. But the upper mids to treble are truly spacious, open and bright. (IEM battle review on his YouTube.)

OK, actually. The treble suddenly drops off, maybe at 10 kHz, then suddenly gets pointy again around 12 kHz, so the treble is a bit crispy: singers' lip-smacking, like chewing, is very audible, and cymbals tizz too. Good, natural timbre. But for me the technicalities are just adequate, the bass lacks punch compared with the Xuan NV, and pushed loud it can get bright too. Not a bad sound though. If you like lots of treble, clean mids and not-very-punchy bass, this works.

New "Ugh, no. Overdone mid-bass, very old-school. Not my tonal bias at all. Dirty in the low-mids, mid-bassy; I don't like it. And 6 kHz is dipped hard too. I think even the GK Kunten has a far better tuning than this."

I don't really like its treble roll-off; it's a bit untidy. But this is more balanced and cleaner, and low notes are heard more clearly than on the S08. Comes with a USB-C cable, of course; its DAC is ordinary and sounds a bit bright compared with switching to a 3.5 mm cable and a DAC like the Shanling UA1 Plus. Soundstage and imaging are still average; it didn't excite me like planars such as the 7Hz Timeless, Raptgo or Tangzu Heyday. But for the price it's OK to collect.

Another planar, another not-so-impressed day. The OG is shouty in the mids; the Pro is warmer but the treble presence at the top is boosted even more. The bass lacks bite: not tidy, not punchy. The mids are OK and pleasant, but even for a planar it doesn't feel spacious enough, and separation isn't great either. Just OK, not that impressive. Plus the nozzle and fit aren't great. Stick to the EW300 and Tangzu Xuan.

Balanced, punchy! "I'd say the driver beats the Inawaken Dawn MS for mid-bass thump: the Inawaken feels slightly slower with more sub-bass rumble, while this is cleaner in the low-mids/mid-bass, faster, with more tactile mid-bass punch. Annoyingly, I still haven't found an IEM with a lower air peak at 10 kHz; this one still has a pointy bit. The peak is fairly narrow, not broad like the Astral's treble, so it's a little hard to notice, but it's there; not too spicy, because the Q (width) isn't wide. If you're open to EQ, go for it, it's safe. Without EQ I think it's still safe. Certainly the upper mids and pointy air are far safer than the Klean SV."

Dawn MS: new, recommended, "the Jansen" "The counter to the Tin C3. Nice fit, full resin, a pretty faceplate. Better, more natural timbre than the C3, even with the C3 on H570 eartips. If you already have a C3, keep it; the improvement may not be big. This has more treble, not as warm as the C3. Even against the Sonus its mid-bass is good; the Sonus has slightly better upper midrange and imaging. But for a single DD this is a killer deal: no need to swap anything, it's already nice. It comes with short and long eartips; swap tips if you want it even better. (IEM battle review on his YouTube.)"

Very neutral, a straight line. The upper mids to lower treble are high; 8 kHz is a bit dangerous because the low end is thin. If you raise the volume to get bass, don't take this: it'll get bright first. Suits people who like neutral to bright. For EQ, see the table on the far right; I made a JM-1 with slightly raised, fun bass. The timbre is nice, really. But I have to recommend things to a broad audience, and general users surely prefer something with bass over neutral, which is why it's hard for me to recommend.

MK II update: more highs, not as warm as the old one. The treble at 10 kHz is clearer and not harsh. The fit is fine too. The cable and eartips are usable, but swapping to a Xinhs SCC cable and H570 eartips helps: more midrange, and tidier mid-bass to sub. With the stock setup the mid-bass is a bit muddy. (Full review on his YouTube.)

Bass and technicalities are actually no problem, but for me it's really lacking. The timbre is very, very metallic. I tried swapping the cable to a Sena and changing eartips: it didn't cure the metallic, iron-like ringing. Such a pity. As usual: when a big, normally expensive brand suddenly makes something cheap, this happens. Weak. Stay with the Xuan NV and EW300.

Semi-open-back. Good technicalities, a spacious, open soundstage. Main minus: a peak at 8 kHz with not much mid-bass; the rumble is a bit shy and lacks weight compared with the Inawaken and C3. But the stage is good: there's air and spaciousness. The 8 kHz can be dangerous for people sensitive to sibilance there who like it loud. Nice fit with the stock Sancai tips. Not very isolating (semi-open design). The price is awkwardly close to the Xuan NV. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

Pleasant, airy, good soundstage, the fit is OK. More balanced and wider than the original C2, and not as bright as the old one. Lovely. There's a USB-C version you can EQ; I got the 3.5 mm, not the USB-C. The cable mic is fine for calls too. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

One of the best EPZ products, and really well priced. A very balanced tuning, with enjoyable timbre, not metallic like the EW200. Clear, with a truly open soundstage feel. If you find the C3 too bassy/warm in the treble, take this. Nice at medium/moderate volume: open, spacious, clear. Not much bass covering the vocals, but not too neutral either. The stock cable and eartips are already good. The C3 KILLER, since the C3 needs at least a tip swap to enjoy. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

Somewhat incoherent; the mids go missing a bit, mainly the low-mids. But the coherency is actually decent; people who don't think much about coherency can enjoy it. Slightly U-shaped, lots of sub, a fair bit of sparkle at the top of the treble. Not my recommendation; go to the Sonus or Inawaken.

V-shaped-ish: recessed mids, fat bass, prominent upper mids, but the treble doesn't sting. Wide for the price. The timbre is a bit unnatural. If you're still Team V-shape and like recessed mids but don't want spiciness and want wide imaging, this is better than the 5-year-old KZ ZS10 Pro. Fun, just an out-of-fashion tuning. I'd love to see CCA tune this config like the C3, Sonus or EM6L.

Brighter than the C3. Suits low/moderate volume; very loud it can sting. Lovely, spacious; one of the grandest, most open IEMs in the upper mids. My only complaint is the MMCX connector: not bad, just fewer options. The fit is OK, but the C3 isolates better and is snugger. Compared with the EW200, the EW200's timbre is metallic and its sub-bass doesn't extend as deep as this.

I think it's overpriced. The design is gorgeous, but the value still loses, especially next to the Tin C3 single DD. At this budget I'd rather suggest the Kiwi Quintet, SR5 or 41T. The bass is lovely, deep and vibrating thanks to the passive radiator: a mature punch, like listening to a good dynamic headphone. The minus is the slightly metallic timbre, a very slightly unnatural iron echo. The upper mids/treble are ordinary. Maybe OK at around 1 million rupiah. The sound itself is lovely, even next to the Oxygen/Origin.

Neutral-warm-ish; the bass isn't as big as the white Kinera Wyvern, which I think is a magic IEM that still competes with this. But here note weight and slow plucks have very audible decay. The fit is nice and small, and the mic is super clear, better than the Kinera Wyvern. Comes with 2 cables: one 3.5 mm with an inline mic, and one very long USB-C cable with a boom mic.

A bit overpriced; maybe at 270k it's still the sweet spot. Better resolution than the TE Gate. The tuning is OK, I think; compared with the first one, the bass has more weight and punch. Treble clarity is still very OK. The fit gets tiring: there's a bump that becomes uncomfortable after a while. Midrange resolution is better than the Gate and Chu 2. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

Great that KZ could make a comeback with the DFi and PR2, with good drivers under a million. Lovely. A real planar (the community has opened it up). The imaging and separation really are like 2-million planar IEMs such as the S12, P1, Zetian Wu etc. Weakness: the tuning is a bit bright at 10–16 kHz and could be piercing in the upper treble, and the planar timbre is a bit unnatural. It needs a lot of power: a big DAC/amp or a desktop DAC/amp.

If you're more into the upper-midrange frequencies; supposedly Moondrop Kato-ish. If you like more bass, this is not for you. Cleaner vocals than the T3 Plus. Could be nasally, but it's fine. A bit blunt in the upper treble.
The tuning is actually safe, but somehow it isn't lively or grand enough. Something like the Dioko still wins on technicalities.

New, a Sony collectible "A very, very comfortable fit, and a unique red/blue colour you shouldn't miss. For audiophiles/hobbyists, the sound isn't trendy: muddy mid-bass, cut upper mids, bright at 5 and 8 kHz, warm air. Pretty odd, and critical JM-1 or modern U-shape audiophiles surely won't like it. It's for monitoring: it needs lots of low-mids so it stays thick and doesn't vanish on stage, masked by the PA and subwoofers. Since I'm not a pro, I scored its tonality from a hobbyist's perspective."

Very similar to the Kinera Wyvern: mid-centric, thick low-mids, just-right punch. A bit airy around 13–15 kHz, though you may not notice because the fit is rather odd. On the graph it looks a bit pointy like the Cadenza 2, but to me the air didn't sound very bright; with EQ I still cut it, only a little. Good. The only minus is the fit: it feels like it floats in the ear, with empty space, and sometimes it pops out for me.

The driver is actually good: satisfying bass and good technicalities. It's just overemphasised at 4–6 kHz, the sibilance region, which you can hear. At low volume it's still safe; at moderate to high volume vocals get very crispy and spicy, and sometimes it bothers the snare drum too.

Now this is better. HE should tune close to this: the safe tuning is warm and balanced rather than bright or too thin/neutral. It competes closely with the Wyvern. The Wyvern is more upper-mid-centric and feels like it loses a little thickness in the low-mids and mids, while this is warmer than the Wyvern in the 2–8 kHz region. The air is about the same. Not very different; if you collect both and have an EQ-capable DAC, it's much the same. But without EQ this sounds thicker in the low-mids and warmer in the upper mids.

Best budget Tangzu "The best Wan'er in terms of sub-bass rumble: very OK. A fair amount of air treble, Tea Pro-style. The most natural timbre at low to moderate volume; too loud and the air treble can surely pierce, but 8 kHz isn't as high as the Cozoy. Cleaner-sounding than the Kinera Wyvern, with bigger sub-bass rumble too; but the Wyvern's treble is warm, so for loud listening the Wyvern is safer. This suits medium volume."

Mic test "BEST IEM at 300k rupiah. A safe, balanced-warm tuning, not spicy. A lovely soundstage, already in the class of 500k IEMs. I feel the treble could be a bit airier, but this is more than enough. Don't get the purple Abyss or the Remaster: muffled, too dark, the upper mids covered. (Review on his YouTube.)"

In the Kinera Wyvern's class. 10 kHz isn't cut as deep as the Wyvern, so it's cleaner and brighter, and fairly bright at 8 kHz, though the upper mids don't mountain up, so it's still safe. If you like clearer: airier and clearer than the Wyvern. Still take the Wyvern if you like it loud and are sensitive at 8 kHz. Either way. The fit is smaller than the Wyvern, but not as small as the Kiwi Belle.

New Tin HiFi "A muddy low-mid tuning, bright from lower treble to air. A bit difficult and experimental. The plasticky timbre is quite noticeable in the highs. Surprisingly, coherency is OK for the budget: still slightly patchy but safe enough that you may not notice. After EQ it can be balanced (see the table on the right), but the plasticky timbre never goes away. At this budget I prefer a single DD, just a single DD."

Still very Tanchjim; from the Bunny to this it's the same story: a gradual mid-bass rise from the very middle, 500 Hz, down to the sub, but small, and bright at 8 kHz. Not my cup of tea. The driver is OK, the technicalities are OK.

Tangzu's first attempt at a BA + DD hybrid. Very weak, roughly like the Tanchjim Kara. The high treble from the BA pierces: shouty, unnatural. Better the Simgot EM6L, or if your budget allows, go straight to the Sound Rhyme SR5.

An ordinary 500k single DD. Safe. Only the treble is grainy, kind of rough. I don't know how to describe it, but you'll know once you compare it with the C3 or Q1 Pro; those two are better. This one wins on accessories: a modular cable with swappable 2.5/4.4 jacks, and swappable nozzle filters that differ only slightly, like the Simgot EA500. METAL BODY: be careful of static shocks. My advice: just get the EPZ Q1 Pro or C3.

DSP "More spacious and open, with a tidier midrange to treble and better clarity, even compared with the DFi. But get the DSP (digital signal processing) version: its USB-C plug is also a DAC that applies an EQ preset directly to the IEM (no setup needed), so it's well balanced. The bass is tidy and deep. Cool. Wider and nicer than the Tin C0, but that's a different price, mate. Detachable 2-pin, so you can still use it if you change cables one day. Best worn straight down; if you customise, my advice is skip the ear hooks. The treble can get a bit sharp at loud volume."

Have a Wan'er SE? Keep it. Don't have one? Fine to buy. The SE has very slightly less bass and is a bit brighter. Against the white Kinera Wyvern I still prefer the Kinera (subjective: warmer, wider in the lows). The cable's ear hook isn't good; my advice is to tear it off: it's stiff and thick and pulls the fit out of the ear. Comes with Sancai eartips.

New, V-shaped basshead "Bass-heavy, V-shaped, but the top of the treble isn't too spicy. The driver's OK; the tonality isn't for me, against the JM-1 trend: the classic V. For basshead lovers. Suits lower volumes."

A slightly upgraded KZ Saga "Good. Slightly less bass than the Saga, even the Balanced version, and the treble isn't higher than the Saga's either (check his squig). Very similar to the Tin C1; the C1 has a little less sub. My note: the low-mids are still a bit much for my taste, but it's OK. The nozzle looks great; hopefully there aren't many imbalance issues from sweat getting stuck in the nozzle. And the part near the ear is plastic, not metal, so hopefully no shocks in houses without grounding."

KILLER BUDGET IEM OF 2025! Verrrry good tonally: well balanced, not V-shaped, cheap. It feels spacious and simply balanced. Moderate-volume lovers will surely like it. Not super punchy or boomy, just balanced. The Bass version adds a little bass and pointier treble; take this over the Bass version. It's actually not very different from the Polaris, just with more weight from mid-bass to sub-bass; I'm sure many people will like it. (Review on his YouTube.)

The nozzle has been improved. The tuning got even more neutral, with even less sub-bass. The tuning is fine if you want something for monitoring without much sub. But I prefer the white Kinera Wyvern, Pro or non-Pro; that one's simply better. The fit is OK and the resin is sturdy. (He notes the tuning feels thick in the sub.) (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

Very good value for its budget, competing with the Chu 2 and Zero 2. I find the treble pleasing too, and not too bright; a bit warm, slightly muddy. Looking at the graph, the Zero 2 at twice the price makes no sense to me, especially as the Zero's fit isn't nice. At around 100k this wins big. I also prefer its tuning to the Castor Bass. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

DSP, mic test "Half the price of the ONE and very close in quality, in a slightly different direction: the One emphasises sub-bass more and has a slightly wider soundstage up top; the low-mids on the C0 are enjoyable, and rock and pop-punk sound fierce. The One wins on fit. But for 200k this is excellent and can beat the DFi too. Any version is OK; the DSP USB-C one is slightly warmer, otherwise the same. You can't change the cable without losing the brand's correction; for the detachable version you need a good cable + a good DAC. If you have the budget, go straight to the C2 if you want to stay with Tin HiFi. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)"

Tin HiFi drivers are never bad; their timbre is always good. Even cheap, it doesn't have the metallic iron ringing in the treble that KZ/CCA still have. Annoyingly the treble roll-off is still a bit pointy (check Fernanda's squig.link), though better than the Saga and Phoenix. But the GK Kunten can definitely rival it.

Extremely limp, weak bass, not just in quantity: even when I boost the bass with EQ, it doesn't kick like other neutral IEMs such as the Arisyn Huo Shu and Moondrop Lan 2 Ref. So I'd say go for the Arisyn instead. Limp, plus an upper-mid-centric, bright tuning. Not recommended from me, by my subjective preference. Tough.

Yet another 300k set. Upper-mid-to-treble-centric. Punchy, but not much bass: very, very little. Very Tanchjim. The driver's treble is a bit rough, an affordable driver: not harsh as in merely boosted in the lower treble/upper mids, but genuinely grainy, rough and less resolving. I prefer the white Kinera Wyvern / Tangzu Wan'er Studio. A bit better than the Chu 2 / TE Gate. For vocal lovers who want less bass. (Full review on his YouTube.)

Skip the Qing/Abyss "The safe Kinera Wyvern compared with the Qing and the purple Abyss: this one's better. It competes closely with the white one, and many people don't like the white colour; here's the answer. Pleasant. Very balanced tonality even pushed loud. Spacious vocals. Separation and imaging are very OK for under 500k. The timbre is also more natural than the white one. The mid-bass is a bit much and the upper mids still a little covered compared with the white, but it's very safe if you want a Wyvern and don't like the white colour."

Mic test "DON'T BUY IT ANY MORE: LOTS OF IMBALANCE PROBLEMS. The tuning isn't V-shaped. The bass quantity isn't overdone. Clear midrange vocals; the presence boost doesn't hurt. Very lively, reverb tails clearly audible, enjoyable punch. Technically still not at the Tin HiFi C3's level, whose cymbals are natural and not harsh; KZ is still slightly rough, but very OK. A good recommendation. There's a tunable version (EQ presets on the IEM body that only raise or lower the bass); maxed out, it still has less bass than the non-tunable DFi. If you like it as neutral as the tunable, better to get the Tin C2. A pity, in my view. Can rival the BLON Z300. Swap eartips to AET08 or Type E. The mid-bass isn't muddy like the BLON; cleaner."

Audiophiles love saying so cheap and you get a planar": overglorifying planars in cheap IEMs happens a lot. The planar timbre is still lacking. Tonally it's nearly identical to the Kunten, just airier and slightly cleaner. At this budget, why not the HE Wenji, Wyvern or Tangzu? Just want the planar validation? Go ahead. (Full review on his YouTube.)"

New Moondrop "A bit more defined, clearer clarity than the 2, as I remember. For separation and stereo-imaging width I'd pick the Wyvern over this. The tonality is a bit muddy in the low-mids; the upper mids are safe, and the air treble isn't piercing. It's dominated by low-mids and upper mids. I've made an EQ for it (table on the right). The main weakness: the cable makes it a bit murky and less open. Swapping to a KBEAR P34 / Hazy solved this, but the cable doesn't seat fully, blocked by the shell. Verus Candy and Xinhs SCC fit."
Mild V, slightly muddy. Not my preference. (Review on his YouTube.)

The fit is a champion, like the Hola: a really good fit for monitoring. Balanced sound. The midrange isn't as revealing as the Wan'er and Salnotes Zero; the emphasis is definitely at the bottom of the sub-bass and the top of the presence treble, a bit like the Hola. But I think the EW100P is better. Tuning-wise I still like the Wan'er, and the Salnotes Zero if you like less bass. But this is not bad at all.

Wow, the Wan'er has extraordinary quality. An enjoyable treble roll-off, clear. The mid-bass punch is OK compared with the Salnotes Zero; the sub-bass isn't as much as the QKZ HBB. Good driver resolution, not plasticky or metallic, though drivers like the Aria/C3 are still slightly better, not far behind. Build quality is very lacking: the nozzle filter comes off easily.

Same old. Still grainy treble, sharp metallic treble. Upper mids down to the sub are safe; the mids are cut a bit deep around maybe 500 Hz. The timbre is still very CCA/KZ. Stay with the GK Kunten or move on to the Wyvern/Wan'er.

There's a switch but it doesn't change much; just get the Bass version. Lovely for bassheads. Similar. A rather V-shaped, very KZ treble. Safe at low volume; a bit higher and it may be sharp. Want warm? Take the QKZ HBB if you're afraid of sharpness. (Review on his YouTube: IEMs from 100k to 1 million rupiah.)

A superb balanced budget IEM with a great tuning. The cable is really bad and makes it bright; replace it per the recommendation in the table on the right. You can change the tuning by sliding its switches with something like a safety pin; I prefer the Balanced tuning. Swap the eartips to Final Audio Type E and it's not bright any more. Lovely. Weakness at this budget: the treble still sounds veiled and the timbre a bit unnatural, but better than the MT1 Pro. No driver flex (where the driver crinkles like plastic when you insert it).

Great for V-shape lovers. The driver quality is good: smooth highs that don't hurt. Very, very safe. Please stop buying cheap KZs if you like V-shape: just this. If you find it too much, take the Tangzu Wan'er.

Mic test "A nice single DD. Balanced, with very smooth treble. A laid-back soundstage. Extended sub-bass, not overdone. Smooth upper mids and treble. Nice pushed fairly loud too. Nice straight-down fit, just don't push it in too deep or the treble disappears. The only weakness is the cable can't be replaced; if it breaks one day it needs recabling (OneZero or Van Jan Cook can do it)."

Unique: 2 drivers, though the BA doesn't really sound like a BA. The mids are a bit recessed, there's lots of sub-bass compared with the Castor Bass, and the sound is a bit spicy, with an 8 kHz peak that's a bit bothersome. What I admire is the cable: thick, with a clear mic too.
Just buy the MT1 Max, unless this is discounted to 50–60k.
Overhyped; I don't like it. The sound is close to the KZ EDX: still pointy and metallic at 8 kHz, with some boxiness at 300–500 Hz.

A single DD with a nice tuning for a piston-shaped earphone like this, compared with cheap Sonys. If you don't like over-ear-hook style earphones, this could be your answer. Really nice, very similar to the Sony MH755, honestly. The driver is genuinely good and the tuning pleasant; it can compete with the Final E1000. Annoyingly, the cable can't be replaced; I'll try whether it can be recabled or made detachable. But sound-quality-wise it's nice, and it could make a birthday gift since the design is really attractive.

Good technicalities, but the bass tuning isn't great, and it's too bright for me. Sorry, I'm just not Team Crinacle tuning; I'm Team BGGAR. If I want to feel the bass I'll surely raise the volume until I get it, but my ears get stabbed by the treble first.

Who knows which TikTok creator made this viral. It's super muffled compared with the white one. If you want a Kinera, get the white one: a far better, very mature tuning, balanced with a little warmth, and good imaging, not veiled like this. Very covered, muffled.

The perfect wireless headphone "The perfect lifestyle wireless headphone. World-class ANC, superb vocal timbre. A 10-band EQ, flexible to set the tonality you want, on a base that's already balanced, with a bit much low-mid around 100–200 Hz. The best vocal timbre I've heard on a wireless headphone, with smooth, velvety highs. The bass isn't as much as the Momentum 4. ANC better than the QC Ultra. Unmatched microphone quality compared with other brands. Really. The best wireless headphone so far, as a wireless (not as a wired). Main weakness: no wired mode over USB-C, though you can use it while charging with Bluetooth on."

2-year warranty "A top-class, best-sounding high-end headphone, suited to people who still want bass. Not neutral like the Stax S3. Its quality is already like a wired closed-back. Lovely, clear microphone, not far from the XM5; the XM5 wins with a lot of wind or in a café, but the Momentum 4 isn't far behind. The FRAUNHOFER SOUND PERSONALISATION IS EXCELLENT!"

God-tier ANC "UNRIVALLED NOISE-CANCELLING HEADPHONES, but overpriced. The sound is balanced, leaning a bit bassy, but EQable. Sennheiser can actually match it on sound alone. The ANC and transparency are truly superb. Maybe at around 4 million rupiah it'd be humane, but at a 5-million budget I'd rather take the Momentum 4 at around 4 million, unless you really want super-amazing noise cancelling. Sound, fit and ANC are above the XM5. (Video review on his YouTube.)"

Best sound under 1 million rupiah "Best sound. The app is still a bit buggy; hopefully a firmware update comes. But once you've settled on your own EQ or another user's (mine included), I think this is the best-sounding: an OK, fun sub-bass extension, clear mids, more powerful volume. Literally the best compared with EarFun, Edifier and Tozo in terms of sound. The mic is OK too. Only the ANC isn't great. (Review on his YouTube.)"

God-tier mic, affordable god-tier ANC "Good overall at an attractive price. Good mic; on the street or in a café the noise reduction gets a bit strong, so it turns robotic. The driver isn't as good as Sennheiser's, though Sony's driver is still OK. It loses badly on battery. ANC + mic are the best. Comfortable. Not for sports. SPOTIFY TAP: an integrated Spotify feature that doesn't just skip songs but switches playlists straight from what you usually listen to."

Low-price ANC, mic + case "You should skip the CH720 and come here. It easily covers a wide audience, especially those who like BASS! Three modes: ULT Off (warm-balanced), ULT 1 (a bass boost I can still enjoy), ULT 2 (overdone, distorted bass). Stay on Off or 1. ANC, mic and fit are better than the Accentum, but I prefer the Accentum's sound (I like clear mids and just don't like basshead). Folds, comes with a case. (Review on his YouTube.)"

Accentum "Great mids, punch, well balanced. Better than the XM5 in terms of sound. The ANC is serious too, good, not a token or fake one like cheap wireless headphones. The cups are a bit smaller than the M4, but they still go around my ears, though fairly snugly. Custom EQ. Done. It can also run wired over USB-C! CHARGE AND USE!"

Best retro on-ear "The best-sounding on-ear: the Sony CH520 loses, the JLab Rewind loses. Against the Moondrop Old Fashioned and Koss KPH40 it competes very well too, since it takes a parametric EQ, which is excellent: I could boost the bass more and cut the slightly airy treble. Weak on the mic, and the drivers can't swivel. Otherwise mostly positive."

Best at a million rupiah, with a very well-balanced sound. Soundcore is usually very V-shaped; these mids are good now. Enough sub-bass, not too much. Decent soundstage. Much cheaper than the Edifier WH950NB and Sony C720, but the quality is really good, I swear. The Edifier's volume is a bit low; this one isn't at all: it's loud without maxing out.

The bass is there, not over-punchy. Long battery. VERY GOOD mic, PARAMETRIC EQ, game mode, theatre mode. Cheap and already good. Almost no weaknesses; at most it's a little less loud with my custom EQ. Comes with a nice case. Good for office workers who can't afford a flagship yet. Silent ANC, no hiss. The Stax S3, by contrast, has no ANC and a weaker mic (read across to the right). This one's still bassy; the Stax is neutral.

Not bad sound: balanced-warm. On-ear fit, good for sports. Outside noise still gets in. Decent microphone. No ANC. A wireless headphone that simply does the job, but the sound really is decent, balanced.

The industry standard for mixing and audiophiles since 1994. You can hear mixing mistakes and shortcomings on it. Excellent. If you're not used to a neutral headphone like this, the bass will feel lacking, but you get to HEAR WHAT THE AUDIO ENGINEER WANTS YOU TO HEAR: listen to the music exactly the way the mixing engineer wants you to hear it. Enjoyably vocal-centric too. The soundstage is narrower than the HD650. TRUST ME, many audiophiles and audio engineers agree: these HD-series headphones are better than other headphones that even cost $2,000. (Review on his YouTube.)

New affordable open-back "Wow, this is really lovely. Compared with the HD560S it has more air, but the fit is much nicer: less swivel trouble, and although the earcups are a bit smaller than the HD560S, for some reason it's just more comfortable: the curve of the pad material, and better headband padding too. This sits below the R70x. Imaging and soundstage are very OK for such a low price. Definitely a very good product. Maybe a bit dark in the upper mids around 3 kHz, but lots of air treble at the top of the presence. Still similar to the R70x, with a more forgiving 8 kHz but a slightly brighter treble on average."

Very neutral, better clarity, and a more open soundstage. Downsides: the fit keeps shifting when I wear it, and it's overpriced for closed-back monitors; all of this can be had from the K361, DT770, even the FiiO FT1, or eveeen the HD280 Pro in the same pro line-up. Only the fit and clamp are roomier than the HD280.

New, recommended "This is really good. It challenges other monitoring headphones like the Beyer DT770, M50x, MDR-7506, or even the Sennheiser HD620S Closed. Very balanced and tidy; good imaging, good, natural timbre. Cool mesh pads, big earcups. Very comfortable for session players monitoring a recording. Deep bass, extended but not overdone/boomy. Sparkly treble, a bit dangerous at 5 kHz; very loud it gets a bit bright. Detachable cable, comes with a nice case."

A good one from Sennheiser. I think the best sound at around 2 million rupiah is this and the K361: the most accurate timbre and sound for reproducing what you record into the DAW. The soundstage is fairly spacious too, and no frequency is too bright. Weaknesses: not detachable (maybe moddable at Guiltorin), and the earpads flake like the MDR-7506's. But this is more than enough compared with the HD620S.

Sony's most legendary professional headphone, since 1991, still made ONLY in Japan. Used for recording monitoring and TV/radio broadcasting. The tuning is boosted quite a lot in the upper mids/treble, but that makes it good for monitoring human voices and mixing mistakes. Yet music is also more fun on it than on any other headphone at the same price. ALL PARTS ARE SERVICEABLE, and many people still mod it to be detachable, swap earpads, headbands etc. Better build quality than the ATH-M50x and M40x.
New "Still neutral, a bit more open-sounding than the AR5000, and fuller-sounding too. Sadly nothing impresses me that much. At this price point I'd much prefer the Audeze MM100."
A bit bright in the lower treble; I don't like it much. The sound is open, like most open-backs, but very bright. My advice: the HD560S instead.

New cheap open-back "The tonality is a bit sharp at 8 kHz, with high upper mids, and the mid-bass to sub-bass is higher than the JT7: more V-shaped, so to speak. But I like the fit, and I really like the price: only 1 million. Paired with a dongle it's still a bit hard to drive, but a SnowSky Melody works; then EQ it (my EQ is at the far right). A proper soundstage for 1 million, a bit held back on a dongle. The dilemma: it's cheap, so recommending a desktop DAC/amp like the DX5 II feels outrageous budget-wise, right? Try the Melody and EQ. High gain!"

We're not sure if it's open, closed or semi-open, but it's surely a very well-tuned neutral headphone, with great vocals. The bass isn't boomy or even boosted. Very comparable to the SHP9500 in tuning, with less bright upper mids.

A good driver, closed-back, but muddy with a lot of mid-bass/low-mids, and the sub-bass rolls off; similar to the KPH40 there, but brighter at 10 kHz. You can EQ it now that the SnowSky Tiny exists, so I treat it like having this headphone with a USB-C end whose EQ I can correct into something really goood. On-ear life changed since the SnowSky Tiny, lol. But it really is very expensive compared with the KPH40's value. The KPH's trick is that it's semi-open: more spacious after EQ. The HD25's cable exits upward, which is unique, and the left earcup can flip forward so it's like wearing one side only. Good for DJing.

They are better than they look, and literally an OPEN-BACK design; the sound is amazing. It needs a bit more power. I had it customised to MMCX at Herz Garage (Tokopedia) to make it detachable, and swapping the cable helped a fair bit, especially 4.4 mm, which carries more power. Wide, open sound, a bit muddy with a lot of bass around 125 Hz; cut it a little and it's spot on. A bit tiring over long sessions because it's on-ear, but they sound nice: balanced, with more mid-bass but open-sounding. I suggest buying a SnowSky Tiny to EQ it: insanely good after EQ with the SnowSky Tiny. (Review on his YouTube.)

Good, balanced, very neutral. Not stinging, nothing weird. Plugged straight into a sound card it's already nice. Comes with a nice hard case. Crazy, I only just learned about this; I tried it at an audio meetup and the value turns out to be excellent.

This sound leans neutral too and works well for mixing. Semi-open-back: it leaks a bit, but not as much as an open-back. Very enjoyable, and one of RTINGS' top 10 for value for money. A bit bright, but very open-sounding.
This is kind of everybody's first headphone among people who mix. Honestly, you're better off with this than some no-name gaming brand. The fit is OK, and it's over-ear and very comfortable.
Better to just take the Audio-Technica S120C: better tonality, safer tuning. Even the Sony ZX310AP is far better. This is very bright; it only wins on the Koss-style scene looks.

New "God-tier, crazily well-packed features: 80-hour battery, AI mic, detachable mic, custom EQ in the phone and desktop apps, an adjustable mixer for sidetone (hearing your own voice + the game), and a lag-free USB-C dongle that plugs into PC, phone and PlayStation."

Sony's gaming line has the H3, H7 and H9, but for value for money just take the H3: much cheaper, no need for wireless, and the mic is far better than the wireless ones. Weakness: no ANC or Bluetooth, but for me that's not even a weakness. There's an app for custom EQ and gain, and it's DISCORD certified. Good mic.

Worth it "Good mic. Balanced-warm sound. The fit is OK. Plenty enough for a newbie, and light on the head. The GSP300 is slightly more neutral, but this doesn't end up bassy either, just balanced-warm. Lovely clarity, imaging and separation. I think it can really compete with wireless ones under a million, or even under 2 million."
